chunks: Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar and Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan — all together from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ibn Muskan, from al-Halabi, who said:
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'My father (peace be upon him) used to give legal rulings and he practiced caution (taqiyya), and we used to fear regarding the prey of falcons and hawks.
But as for now, we do not fear, and we do not declare their prey permissible, except when the ritual slaughter (dhakah) is performed upon it.
For it is in the Book of Ali (peace be upon him) that God, Mighty and Majestic, says: "And what you have trained of hunting animals, trained ones" — (this is) regarding dogs.

key_terms.الصُّقُور: Hawks (singular: saqr); predatory birds used in falconry
key_terms.الْبُزَاة: Falcons (singular: baz); birds of prey used for hunting
key_terms.الْجَوَارِح: Hunting animals (literally 'those that wound/catch'); the term in Quran 5:4 that the Imam specifies refers only to dogs
key_terms.تَقِيَّة: Taqiyya — precautionary dissimulation practiced under threat or oppression; here the Imam's father gave cautious rulings for fear of Umayyad persecution
key_terms.ذَكَاة: Ritual slaughter; the prescribed Islamic method of killing an animal to render it lawful for consumption
key_terms.صَيْد: Prey; the act of hunting and what is hunted
key_terms.كِتَابُ عَلِيٍّ: The Book of Ali (AS) — a written record dictated by the Prophet (SAWW) to Imam Ali (AS), preserved among the Imams and referenced frequently in jurisprudential matters

ai.seo_question: Is prey caught by falcons and hawks permissible to eat in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) explains an evolution in legal position regarding hunting with birds of prey (falcons and hawks). His father, Imam al-Baqir (AS), had previously issued cautious rulings under taqiyya due to Umayyad oppression. Now freed from such fear, Imam al-Sadiq clarifies the definitive ruling: the prey of falcons and hawks is not permissible unless one catches the animal alive and performs ritual slaughter (dhakah). The justification comes from the Book of Ali (AS), which cites Quran 5:4 — the verse about hunting animals trained by humans — as specifically pertaining to dogs (not birds), meaning birds' prey requires slaughter unlike dogs' prey.
